     the sentence: "@Condit2002 found...". -->

Tropical forests hold more tree species than any other terrestrial
ecosystem, and which of them grow together changes from place to place, even
within a single forest. How fast it changes -- beta diversity -- and how much
of that change follows the habitat are central questions of tropical
ecology [@Condit2002].

The composition of an assemblage -- which species, and how many of each -- is
usually compared between sites through a dissimilarity, such as Bray-Curtis.
Its relationship with the environment is then tested with a permutational
multivariate analysis of variance [PERMANOVA, @Anderson2001], and shown with
an ordination such as a non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS). Because a
PERMANOVA can confound a difference in the mean composition of the groups with
a difference in how variable they are [@Warton2012], it is accompanied by a
test of the homogeneity of their dispersions [PERMDISP, @Anderson2006].

Here we use the trees of the 50-ha plot of Barro Colorado Island to ask two
questions: does the number of tree species differ among the habitats of the
forest, and does the composition of the tree assemblage?
